lead: Anchoring well means choosing the spot, laying enough chain and proving that the anchor holds. In harbour the same care goes into your lines.

qa.q: Which bay should I anchor in overnight when the wind is forecast to change?
qa.a: Choose shelter from the **forecast** wind, not the present one: a bay open to it becomes a lee shore, so move while it is light. Drop on sand or mud, not on weed or rock.

blocks.p: Plan your way out before dark.

fig.note: Forecast: wind backing south overnight, F5

blocks.cap: Only A lies under the land when the wind goes south.

blocks.p: The chart names the seabed: **S** sand and **M** mud let an anchor dig in, **Wd** weed, **R** rock and **Co** coral do not. Drop on pale sand, never on dark seagrass, and clear of a submarine cable, a magenta wavy line.

head: Anchor
Where it works
rows: Sand and mud; may not reset when the pull reverses

sections.title: How much chain to let out

qa.q: How much anchor chain should I let out for the depth I'm in?
qa.a: On all chain, a **scope** of at least 4:1 in settled weather and 5:1 to 7:1 in strong wind; chain and rope needs 6:1 to 8:1. Measure from depth at high water plus bow height.

blocks.p: **Scope** compares the length of rode with the height from the bow roller to the seabed: depth at high water plus bow height. An anchor holds only while the pull is nearly horizontal; a short chain lifts the shank and pulls it out. 4:1 means 4 m of chain per metre: 5 m of water and a 1 m bow need 24 m.

The chain's weight on the bottom does much of the holding; a rope rode still needs a few metres of chain at the anchor against chafe. More scope widens the **swinging circle**: its radius is about the chain along the bottom plus the boat's length. Anchor among boats of your size and scope, so you all swing alike.

labels: rock is 45 m from your anchor

blocks.cap: The stern can swing 52 m from the anchor, past the rock.

sections.title: Stop, let go, dig it in

qa.q: How do I check my anchor is holding right after I drop it?
qa.a: Reverse gently to dig it in and watch a **transit** abeam, two fixed marks ashore in line: steady transit and taut chain, it holds; opening transit and juddering chain, it is skating, so try another spot.

list: Approach slowly, head to wind, and stop over the spot.
Let go as she starts to drift astern, and pay out only as fast as she falls back: chain piled on the anchor fouls it.
Reverse gently to dig it in, then build up to about 1,500 rpm for a while; over rock go easy, it can jam.
Watch a **transit** abeam, two fixed marks ashore in line. Steady transit, taut chain: it holds. Opening transit, juddering chain: it is skating, so try another spot.

blocks.p: In clear water, snorkel over it. In gusts a nylon **snubber** from a bow cleat to the chain spares the windlass; a catamaran rigs a bridle from both bows.

qa.q: How can I tell at night whether my anchor is dragging?
qa.a: Set a GPS **anchor alarm** centred on the anchor, its radius the chain plus the boat's length. On the plotter, swinging draws an arc; a straight track downwind means you are dragging.

blocks.p: If the **anchor alarm** sounds, check transits, track and depth first. Swinging draws an arc; a straight line downwind is dragging.

fig.note: Your GPS track over the last hour

blocks.cap: Loops while she swings, then a straight track as she drags.

blocks.p: If you drag, start the engine and motor up to take the strain, then re-anchor or leave. If a neighbour drags down on you, wake her crew with horn and torch; engine on, fenders out. In strong wind set an anchor watch.

head: Two anchors
What for
rows: Bahamian moor: two bow anchors 180° apart

qa.q: How do I raise the anchor without straining the windlass?
qa.a: Let the **engine** move the boat: motor slowly up the chain so the windlass only takes in slack, lock it off with the chain up and down, and break the anchor out by motoring gently ahead.

blocks.p: Agree hand signals first: the bow crew points along the chain. Motor slowly up it so the windlass only takes in slack. With the chain up and down, lock it off and break the anchor out by motoring gently ahead. Then set the chain stopper and lash it.

head: Problem
Answer
rows: Pull it out backwards: a trip line on the crown, or from the other side
Hold their chain on a slip line, lower yours clear
Lay the kedge by dinghy towards deep water and winch off

qa.q: How do I moor stern-to on a town quay in the Med with my own anchor?
qa.a: Drop the anchor three to four boat lengths out, reverse in straight so your chain does not cross the neighbours', and take two **stern lines** ashore. Get sternway early: prop walk is strongest from rest.

blocks.p: On a town quay you lie **stern-to**: the anchor holds the bow, two lines the stern. Once she has sternway, the rudder steers.

In a cross wind drop upwind of the berth's line. The **windward stern line** goes ashore first when you arrive and comes off last when you leave. In surge, ease the stern lines and haul in chain to sit further off. Ferry berths stay clear.

fig.note: Wind on the beam of the berth, F4

blocks.cap: From B the chain holds the bow up to windward.

blocks.p: A **lazy line** replaces the anchor: make it fast at the end away from the quay, and stay in neutral until it is clear of the propeller. In a cove a shore line holds the stern: lead it round a rock and back aboard, to slip from the deck.

sections.title: Breast lines hold, springs stop the surge

qa.q: Which mooring lines stop my boat surging back and forth alongside a pontoon?
qa.a: The **springs**, which run diagonally, stop her surging; bow and stern lines, and breast lines square to the pontoon, hold her in. Where the level changes, leave the lines long and slack.

blocks.p: Wind off the berth: come in steeper, get a line from the stern or midships cleat on fast and motor gently ahead against it to hold her in, then the bow line; to leave, just let go. Wind onto it: stop parallel a metre off; to leave, motor ahead against a bow spring, bow fendered, until the stern swings out. In a raft, take your own lines ashore and cross by the foredeck.
Approach a **mooring buoy** into the wind. Its pick-up line only lifts the ring: lie to your own line, from a bow cleat through the ring and back to the same cleat.

fig.note: Through the ring and back to the same cleat
